questions.question: What were new admins worried about at the Invite your team step?

seeded.answer: New admins were anxious at the “Invite your team” step because they were unsure whether the invites would be sent immediately or only after the entire wizard was submitted. They worried that invites might be sent before they were ready, potentially exposing a mistake to their team. This hesitation was the longest stall in the onboarding flow and was noted in the journey map, synthesis, and topline summaries.

questions.question: Which onboarding steps are required, and which can be skipped?

seeded.answer:
The onboarding wizard is defined in the user‑flows document as a six‑step sequence.
Step 1 – Signup (required)
Step 2 – Basics (workspace name, team size) (required)
Step 3 – Connect calendar (required) – marked explicitly as required in the v2 flow and flagged as the biggest drop‑off point in the funnel export [1][2]
Step 4 – Invite your team (required) – shows a draft/not‑sent state and is still required before finishing the wizard [1]
Step 5 – Preferences (required)
Step 6 – Review & finish (required)

None of the steps are optional; all must be completed before the wizard can be finished. Participants in the usability tests attempted to skip step 3 because it was not clearly marked as required, but the design documentation confirms that all six steps are mandatory.

questions.question: What did nurses want from the citations in the prior auth drafts?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted the citations to show the exact chart text that supported each claim in the AI‑drafted justification, so they could verify the source themselves. They described this as “show your work” and wanted inline source citations that linked to specific chart‑text spans rather than just section headers. In the v1 test, participants said they needed to see the chart text behind each suggestion to confirm accuracy and avoid payer denials. In the v2 test, nurses actively clicked at least one citation to verify it before accepting, describing the feature as “appropriately fast” and not frictional. This requirement was identified as a durable need in the synthesis and was addressed by adding inline source citations that resolve to specific chart‑text spans in the updated service topology. [1][2][3][4]

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

Consider limiting initial pilot scope to 'straightforward' case types the nurses themselves can help define, deferring complex cases.

questions.question: How were sound-alike medication names handled?

seeded.answer: Sound‑like medication names were treated as a separate error class after GA. The GA‑candidate round decided to monitor them rather than block launch, relying on the existing low‑confidence underline to surface them generically. A dedicated flag was then designed and tested. The flag is a small amber pill‑shaped badge placed inline immediately after the medication name, distinct in shape and color from the low‑confidence underline, with a short on‑hover/on‑tap label: “Possible sound‑alike medication name — verify before signing” [1]. In a moderated usability test with six clinicians (physicians and nurse practitioners) seeded with known sound‑alike pairs, five of six participants correctly identified the flag as a distinct signal from generic low confidence, but two participants reported that the flag’s specificity made them trust unflagged lines more than they should, indicating a risk of over‑trust [2]. The design therefore requires additional UI cues to counter that over‑trust. The overall strategy shifted from a generic confidence highlight to a distinct, actionable flag for sound‑like medication names, with ongoing monitoring and refinement post‑GA.

questions.question: What does the step 3 wireframe show?

seeded.answer: The sources do not contain a wireframe for step 3. They do, however, describe step 3’s role and user experience. Step 3, “Connect calendar,” is marked as required in the onboarding flow logic [1] and is the single largest drop‑off point in the funnel, contributing more incomplete sign‑ups than any other step [2]. Users frequently misread it as optional, with 2 of 3 participants in sessions 1–3 attempting to skip it, and all participants in sessions 1–3 pausing at step 4 because they were unsure whether invites would be sent immediately or after completion [3][4].

seeded.answer: The surveys do not report an overall burnout rate for clinicians. They do, however, quantify documentation burden as the top self‑selected burnout driver: 52 % of physicians identified it as the #1 contributor, ahead of patient volume (31 %) and administrative meetings (12 %) [1][2]. The data also shows that 64 % of physicians regularly complete after‑hours charting, averaging 1.2 hours per day [1]. No source provides a direct percentage of clinicians experiencing burnout.

questions.question: How aware were staff of the Compass AI initiatives?

seeded.answer: The awareness of Compass AI initiatives varied markedly between staff groups. In the all‑staff AI readiness pulse survey, only 34 % of non‑clinical staff reported being aware that Compass AI initiatives were underway, whereas 71 % of clinical staff reported awareness, indicating a significant internal communication gap that may need to be addressed before any administrative‑focused pilots go live.
